claims.assertion: The driven route was 10.7 km against an optimal 8.4 km, +2.3 km (+27%), and the meter therefore billed more distance units than the shortest and most direct route would have (F1).

There are no in-app chat messages at all, so the rider never agreed in writing to this route and there is no rider message predating the segment (F7); the driver's written statement that he followed the GPS (F8) is a statement, and the record of F3 plus the driver's own admission that the device 'rerouted' shows the deviation occurred without the rider's consent.

No incident, roadwork, blockage or heavy-traffic event was recorded near the route during the trip window, and conditions were band 4 (30–39 km/h) on Ayer Rajah Expressway and band 5 (40–49 km/h) on Jurong Town Hall Road with fair weather (F11, F9, F10, F12); speeds in bands 4–5 are not the band 1–2 'severe congestion' status, so the driver has no reasonable-cause exemption under RD-4.

Because this is a metered RydeTAXI trip, the unexempted segment's extra mileage entered the fare: the billing fact states an excess distance charge of $3.26 (2.31 km × $1.4097/km, the trip's distance fare ÷ distance km) (F4, F6).

The refund should be the unexempted segment's extra distance valued at the trip's own per-km rate: 2.13 km × $1.4097/km = $3.00 SGD (rounded to the cent), which is within, not equal to, the $3.26 the meter charged for excess distance (F3, F4).

The driver's 90-day record shows 4 disputes with 2 upheld, both route disputes (F14); this case makes the deviation 'repeated' under RD-6, so an account flag is also warranted. The rider's own clean record (0 upheld disputes, F13) is context only and is not relied on for the finding.

weaknesses: The driver's statement that 'the GPS sent me; it rerouted' (F8) is an attempt to bring the case under RD-4 / RD-5 as a navigation-driven reroute, and the record shows no counter-message from the rider because there was no chat at all (F7) — the judge could read the silence as the rider simply not objecting, though no message can satisfy RD-5's 'before you go' requirement.

F3 shows the segment left the optimal route by up to 954 m and lasted four minutes; a court could treat that as a brief navigation artefact rather than a deliberate deviation, and F1's own figures produce a billed excess of $3.26 for 2.31 km, slightly more than the $3.00 I claim, so the driver may argue the difference between fare-excess and the segment sum is unrecoverable route-corridor mileage under RD-2.

The traffic records placing band 4 and band 5 on named roads (F9, F10) do not tell us which road the optimal route used or which road the driver actually took; the driver could use F9 to argue 'slow traffic justified another way', even though neither band reaches the band 1–2 severe-congestion level RD-4(b) describes.

There is exactly one off-route segment on the record: 12:12–12:16, 2.93 km driven where the optimal route covers 0.80 km, adding 2.13 km and straying up to 954 m from the optimal route (F3); the +2.3 km overall excess in F1 is therefore essentially this single segment, not a trip-long pattern of detours.

The chat record contains no rider message at all before the segment started at 12:12 (F7), so there is no rider message that could constitute consent to the route taken and no rider-named stop; the segment is therefore uncontested on consent and my client does not resist a finding that this segment is unexcused.

The driver's post-trip statement that he 'went where the GPS sent me' (F8) is not relied on as an excuse: it is a claim made after the trip, and no traffic incident on the optimal route is recorded during the trip window (F11), so no RD-4 justification exists for the segment.

The traffic picture during the trip window shows Ayer Rajah Expressway at speed band 4 (30–39 km/h) and Jurong Town Hall Road at band 5 (40–49 km/h) with fair weather (F9, F10, F12), i.e. moderate congestion only and below the band 1/2 severe-congestion level, so it corroborates that the segment was avoidable.

The refund the rider seeks must be measured from the meter: the fare sheet bills the excess distance at this trip's own per-km rate, 2.31 km × $1.4097/km = $3.26 (F4), so any awarded amount is $3.26 and not the $6-plus implied by comparing a quoted 8 km with an 11 km meter reading.

Only the segment's extra distance is refundable; the spread between total actual distance and the sum of the segments is corridor map-matching and cannot be claimed, and no surcharge was added (no surge, waiting fee $0.00) beyond the meter components of F6.

This case does not warrant a flag_account escalation: the record has one single off-route segment with no pattern over the trip (F3), and the driver's 90-day profile shows 963 trips against 2 upheld route disputes (F14), facts which cannot by themselves establish anything about this trip.

Nothing in the record reaches SAFE-1 or SAFE-2: the complaint is a fare dispute, the chat is absent (F7) and the driver's statement (F8) contains no threat, harassment or dangerous-driving allegation, so the case can be decided on RD-1/RD-2 without referral.

weaknesses: The GPS record is against my client on the core point: F3 shows a 2.93 km stretch at 12:12–12:16 where the optimal route covers 0.80 km, adding 2.13 km and reaching 954 m off the optimal route; F1's +2.3 km (+27%) and F2's +2.7 min excess over estimate sit on top of it, so the rider will argue an unexcused deviation under RD-1/RD-2.

There is no rider message before the segment to lean on (F7) and my client's statement (F8) admits the reroute without documenting that the GPS ever proposed it, which under RD-5/G11 leaves no consent and no recorded justification.

The Ayer Rajah Expressway band 4 reading (F9) is a speed band on the optimal route during the trip window; the rider may use it to argue there was congestion and my client may use it under RD-4, but a single band fact is not sufficient for an exemption and cuts both ways.

The driver's 90-day profile shows 2 prior upheld route disputes (F14); the rider will point to RD-6 and ask for a flag_account, which I argue against on the ground that profile facts cannot decide this trip and this trip shows only one segment (F3).

actions.detail: account action is never automatic; queued for Ryde review

what_would_change: Had an LTA incident been recorded on the stretch F3 replaced, before it started, RD-4 would exempt it (−$3.00).

claims.assertion: The driven route was 10.7 km against an optimal 8.4 km, +2.3 km (+27%), and the meter therefore billed more distance units than the shortest and most direct route would have (F1).

The trip recorded one off-route segment, 12:12–12:16, in which 2.93 km were driven where the optimal route covers 0.80 km, adding 2.13 km and leaving the optimal route by up to 954 m (F3); this segment is not covered by any exemption, so it is an unexempted deviation under RD-1.

There are no in-app chat messages at all, so the rider never agreed in writing to this route and there is no rider message predating the segment (F7); the driver's written statement that he followed the GPS (F8) is a statement, and the record of F3 plus the driver's own admission that the device 'rerouted' shows the deviation occurred without the rider's consent.

No incident, roadwork, blockage or heavy-traffic event was recorded near the route during the trip window, and conditions were band 4 (30–39 km/h) on Ayer Rajah Expressway and band 5 (40–49 km/h) on Jurong Town Hall Road with fair weather (F11, F9, F10, F12); speeds in bands 4–5 are not the band 1–2 'severe congestion' status, so the driver has no reasonable-cause exemption under RD-4.

Because this is a metered RydeTAXI trip, the unexempted segment's extra mileage entered the fare: the billing fact states an excess distance charge of $3.26 (2.31 km × $1.4097/km, the trip's distance fare ÷ distance km) (F4, F6).

The refund should be the unexempted segment's extra distance valued at the trip's own per-km rate: 2.13 km × $1.4097/km = $3.00 SGD (rounded to the cent), which is within, not equal to, the $3.26 the meter charged for excess distance (F3, F4).

The driver's 90-day record shows 4 disputes with 2 upheld, both route disputes (F14); this case makes the deviation 'repeated' under RD-6, so an account flag is also warranted. The rider's own clean record (0 upheld disputes, F13) is context only and is not relied on for the finding.

weaknesses: The driver's statement that 'the GPS sent me; it rerouted' (F8) is an attempt to bring the case under RD-4 / RD-5 as a navigation-driven reroute, and the record shows no counter-message from the rider because there was no chat at all (F7) — the judge could read the silence as the rider simply not objecting, though no message can satisfy RD-5's 'before you go' requirement.

F3 shows the segment left the optimal route by up to 954 m and lasted four minutes; a court could treat that as a brief navigation artefact rather than a deliberate deviation, and F1's own figures produce a billed excess of $3.26 for 2.31 km, slightly more than the $3.00 I claim, so the driver may argue the difference between fare-excess and the segment sum is unrecoverable route-corridor mileage under RD-2.

The traffic records placing band 4 and band 5 on named roads (F9, F10) do not tell us which road the optimal route used or which road the driver actually took; the driver could use F9 to argue 'slow traffic justified another way', even though neither band reaches the band 1–2 severe-congestion level RD-4(b) describes.

claims.assertion: The trip is RydeTAXI and metered (F6), so the fare follows the meter rather than the app's 8.4 km quote, which means only meter distance units attributable to an unexcused segment can be refunded, not the whole gap between the quoted and actual distance.

There is exactly one off-route segment on the record: 12:12–12:16, 2.93 km driven where the optimal route covers 0.80 km, adding 2.13 km and straying up to 954 m from the optimal route (F3); the +2.3 km overall excess in F1 is therefore essentially this single segment, not a trip-long pattern of detours.

The chat record contains no rider message at all before the segment started at 12:12 (F7), so there is no rider message that could constitute consent to the route taken and no rider-named stop; the segment is therefore uncontested on consent and my client does not resist a finding that this segment is unexcused.

The driver's post-trip statement that he 'went where the GPS sent me' (F8) is not relied on as an excuse: it is a claim made after the trip, and no traffic incident on the optimal route is recorded during the trip window (F11), so no RD-4 justification exists for the segment.

The traffic picture during the trip window shows Ayer Rajah Expressway at speed band 4 (30–39 km/h) and Jurong Town Hall Road at band 5 (40–49 km/h) with fair weather (F9, F10, F12), i.e. moderate congestion only and below the band 1/2 severe-congestion level, so it corroborates that the segment was avoidable.

The refund the rider seeks must be measured from the meter: the fare sheet bills the excess distance at this trip's own per-km rate, 2.31 km × $1.4097/km = $3.26 (F4), so any awarded amount is $3.26 and not the $6-plus implied by comparing a quoted 8 km with an 11 km meter reading.

Only the segment's extra distance is refundable; the spread between total actual distance and the sum of the segments is corridor map-matching and cannot be claimed, and no surcharge was added (no surge, waiting fee $0.00) beyond the meter components of F6.

This case does not warrant a flag_account escalation: the record has one single off-route segment with no pattern over the trip (F3), and the driver's 90-day profile shows 963 trips against 2 upheld route disputes (F14), facts which cannot by themselves establish anything about this trip.

Nothing in the record reaches SAFE-1 or SAFE-2: the complaint is a fare dispute, the chat is absent (F7) and the driver's statement (F8) contains no threat, harassment or dangerous-driving allegation, so the case can be decided on RD-1/RD-2 without referral.

weaknesses: The GPS record is against my client on the core point: F3 shows a 2.93 km stretch at 12:12–12:16 where the optimal route covers 0.80 km, adding 2.13 km and reaching 954 m off the optimal route; F1's +2.3 km (+27%) and F2's +2.7 min excess over estimate sit on top of it, so the rider will argue an unexcused deviation under RD-1/RD-2.

There is no rider message before the segment to lean on (F7) and my client's statement (F8) admits the reroute without documenting that the GPS ever proposed it, which under RD-5/G11 leaves no consent and no recorded justification.

The Ayer Rajah Expressway band 4 reading (F9) is a speed band on the optimal route during the trip window; the rider may use it to argue there was congestion and my client may use it under RD-4, but a single band fact is not sufficient for an exemption and cuts both ways.
